document.preferred_name: MlaA/VacJ outer-membrane phospholipid transport lipoproteins, plus a divergent alpha/beta-hydrolase-fold subfamily of unknown function
document.summary: Bacterial family defined by the MlaA (VacJ) domain (InterPro IPR007428). Its dominant subfamily, SF3, is MlaA itself: the outer-membrane lipoprotein of the Mla intermembrane phospholipid transport system of diderm bacteria. In Escherichia coli MlaA (P76506) is lipid-anchored in the inner leaflet of the outer membrane, forms a complex with the osmoporins OmpC/OmpF, and is a monomeric alpha-helical protein with a central amphipathic channel through which phospholipids from the outer leaflet are moved towards the periplasm and handed to the soluble carrier MlaC; loss of MlaA leads to phospholipid accumulation in the outer leaflet and envelope permeability defects. Shigella VacJ (P43262), Haemophilus MlaA (P44042) and the Pseudomonas VacJ proteins are orthologs. Many Pseudomonas genomes encode two or three SF3 paralogs (Pseudomonas putida KT2440 has PP_2163/VacJ Q88KX6, the Mla-operon-unlinked exemplar, and PP_1737 Q88M38), whose individual roles have not been resolved. The second subfamily, SF1 ("AB HYDROLASE-1 DOMAIN-CONTAINING PROTEIN"), is a distinct group of roughly 430-residue, signal-peptide-bearing proteins that carry an alpha/beta-hydrolase fold signature and the InterPro MlaA entry but no Pfam MlaA (PF04333) match; they occur mainly in Pseudomonadota, Thermodesulfobacteriota and Fusobacteriota, are widely mis-named "serine/threonine protein kinase" or "PrkA" by automatic naming, and have no experimental characterization. In P. putida KT2440 the SF1 member PP_1738 (Q88M37) is encoded next to the SF3 paralog PP_1737. InterPro counts 7482 proteins in 8045 taxa (integrated entry IPR007428); the fetched entries.csv holds only the 8 reviewed members, all SF3.
document.coherence_reason: SF3 (MlaA/VacJ) is functionally coherent and accounts for the large majority of the family (about 6900 of 7479 UniProt members carry the SF3 assignment). SF1 is the exception: a longer protein with an alpha/beta-hydrolase-fold region, no Pfam MlaA domain hit, and no experimental data, so the MlaA transport function cannot be assumed for it. The single PAINT gain (GO:0120010 at PTN001247191) sits on the SF3 root and PAINT TreeGrafter records no annotation on any of the five SF1 nodes, so SF1 inherits nothing today.

document.preferred_name: MlaC/Ttg2D periplasmic phospholipid carrier of the Mla system
document.summary: Soluble periplasmic phospholipid-binding proteins of the Mla intermembrane phospholipid transport system of diderm bacteria (InterPro IPR008869, MlaC/ttg2D; Pfam PF05494). MlaC carries glycerophospholipid in a hydrophobic pocket and shuttles it across the periplasm between the outer-membrane OmpC/F-MlaA complex and the MlaD hexamer of the inner-membrane MlaFEDB ABC transporter. E. coli MlaC (P0ADV7) is the reference: its loss causes outer-leaflet phospholipid accumulation, it binds MlaA and MlaD directly, and reconstituted assays show phospholipid transfer between MlaC and MlaFEDB that ATP hydrolysis biases in the retrograde (outer-to-inner membrane) direction, although spontaneous anterograde transfer has also been reported. The Pseudomonas orthologs are named Ttg2D (P. aeruginosa Q9HVW4; P. putida KT2440 Q88P91, crystal structures 4FCZ and 5UWB); P. aeruginosa Ttg2D binds two diacyl glycerophospholipids or one cardiolipin. The family is a single PANTHER subfamily (SF1) and spans Pseudomonadota (Gamma-, Beta- and Alphaproteobacteria), Campylobacterota, Myxococcota, Thermodesulfobacteriota and other diderm phyla. InterPro counts 6699 proteins in 8048 taxa; the fetched entries.csv holds the 4 reviewed members.
document.coherence_reason: One subfamily, one fold and one role. Experimental data from two distant gammaproteobacterial lineages (E. coli MlaC and P. aeruginosa Ttg2D) agree on periplasmic phospholipid binding and carriage, and the structure from Ralstonia (PDB 2qgu, the InterPro representative) and Pseudomonas putida show the same lipid-binding fold. No member is known to have a different function.

document.preferred_name: ATP-binding (nucleotide-binding domain) subunits of MCE-type lipid transport systems: MlaF of the diderm-bacterial Mla pathway, mycobacterial Mkl/MceG, and plant TGD3
document.summary: Small, stand-alone ABC nucleotide-binding domains (~260-360 aa, a single P-loop NTPase/ABC_tran module with no fused transmembrane domain) that energize lipid transport across a two-membrane envelope. The best-characterized member is Escherichia coli MlaF, which dimerizes at the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane within the MlaFEDB complex: two MlaF ATPases pair with two copies of the MlaE permease (PTHR30188) and an MlaD (MCE) hexamer (PTHR33371), with the STAS-domain protein MlaB bound to each MlaF. The same three-component architecture recurs in two settings that define the family's functional boundaries. In mycobacteria the single ATPase Mkl/MceG (Rv0655) serves several Mce transporters whose substrates are not phospholipids: Mce1 imports host fatty acids and Mce4 imports cholesterol, and MceG is both the shared energizer and a stability factor for both. In plants and algae the orthologous ATPase TGD3 works with the TGD1 permease and the TGD2 MCE protein at the chloroplast inner envelope, importing ER-derived lipid (phosphatidic acid) toward thylakoid lipid synthesis; TGD3 is stromal rather than periplasmic, has measured basal ATPase activity, and a tgd3 mutant accumulates oligogalactolipids and triacylglycerols. So the conserved property of the family is the ATPase that drives an MCE-type lipid translocator; what varies is the lipid, the compartment pair, and whether the system runs toward the inner membrane or away from it. PANTHER's family name is taken from the plant member and is a poor description of the family as a whole, which is overwhelmingly bacterial: the InterPro slice records 17489 proteins across 11882 proteomes in three subfamilies, while the fetched entries.csv covers only the 10 UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot members (six enterobacterial/Haemophilus MlaF, three mycobacterial Mkl, and Arabidopsis TGD3).
document.coherence_reason: Every member is the nucleotide-binding subunit of an MCE-type lipid transport system, and the generic terms (ATP hydrolysis activity, lipid transport) are safe throughout. Two identified groups diverge in what is transported and where. The mycobacterial Mkl/MceG proteins (inside SF6, alongside MlaF) energize cholesterol and fatty-acid importers, so phospholipid-specific terms do not hold for them. The plant/algal TGD3 clade (SF3) acts in the chloroplast stroma on ER-derived plastid lipid import, so neither the bacterial plasma-membrane complex term nor the diderm-envelope intermembrane-transfer term applies; PAINT already handles that by restricting the corresponding node to taxon 2 (Bacteria). SF4 ("AMINO ACID ABC TRANSPORTER ATP-BINDING PROTEIN") carries a name implying a different substrate class altogether, but no member of it could be verified in the fetched entries or in UniProt queries restricted to model organisms, so its divergence is recorded as unassessed rather than asserted.

node_assessments.assessment_reason: Defensible where it is seeded and wrong at the edges. The seed is E. coli MlaF, which carries an IDA to this term from the MlaFEDB structural and transport work (PMID:33199922), so the assertion reflects a curator's decision to attribute the complex's transfer activity to its ATP-binding subunit. But the node is the whole family root: the same IBA reaches the mycobacterial Mkl/MceG proteins, whose transporters move cholesterol (Mce4) and fatty acids (Mce1) rather than phospholipids, and it reaches the SF3 bacterial paralogs that are not part of an mla operon at all. The branch that needs an IRD is the actinobacterial Mkl/MceG clade; a generic lipid term (GO:0006869, already asserted at this same node) is what those members should keep. No affected_subfamilies are named because the boundary runs inside SF6, which holds MlaF and Mkl together, so a subfamily-level exclusion would wrongly strip the reference protein's own clade. A second, broader caveat for a future PAINT curator: a phospholipid *transfer activity* - carrying a lipid through an aqueous phase in a hydrophobic pocket - is performed by MlaC and by the MlaD hexamer, not by a cytoplasmic ATPase, so the term is arguably a complex-level attribution throughout this family. That is a question about the seed annotation rather than about node placement, and it is recorded here rather than acted on.

node_assessments.assessment_reason: The problem is the term choice, not the node position. GO:1990531 is defined as a protein complex that functions as a phospholipid-translocating P-Type ATPase, i.e. a P4-ATPase flippase complex. Every member of this family is instead the nucleotide-binding subunit of an ABC transporter, so no descendant of this node is part of a P-type ATPase complex and the seed cannot support the term at any node. The seed annotation itself (E. coli MlaF, IPI to the MlaFEDB complex, PMID:27529189) correctly records membership in a transporter complex; what is wrong is the complex type chosen for it, and the IBD carries that error to every bacterial descendant - the Pseudomonas, Haemophilus and Aquifex MlaF proteins and the actinobacterial Mkl/MceG ATPases of the Mce1 and Mce4 importers. GO:0043190 (ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter complex) is the term that fits, and it holds family-wide. The completed E. coli mlaD and mlaE gene reviews make exactly this replacement. No affected_subfamilies are named because the term is inapplicable throughout rather than in one clade; the taxon-2 scope is incidental here, although it does keep the term off plant TGD3.

supported_by.supporting_text: MlaE and MlaF constitute the core components of the ABC transporter and are predicted to form the transmembrane domains (TMDs) and nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), respectively (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2009).

document.preferred_name: MlaE/YrbE/TGD1 transmembrane permease subunits of MCE-type lipid transport systems
document.summary: Small polytopic inner-membrane permeases (~260-350 aa, five transmembrane helices in the resolved core) that form the transmembrane domain of MCE-type lipid transporters. The reference member, Escherichia coli MlaE (also called YrbE), sits at the centre of the MlaFEDB complex: two copies of MlaE pair with two MlaF ATPases (PTHR43023) on the cytoplasmic side and with the MlaD (MCE) hexamer (PTHR33371) on the periplasmic side, and cryo-EM shows a continuous lipid pathway running from the MlaE substrate-binding site through MlaD into the periplasm. MlaE's fold is related to the transmembrane domains of MacB and LptFG rather than to classical ABC importers. The family's three functional settings mirror those of its ATPase and MCE partners. In diderm bacteria the Mla permease handles phospholipids as part of outer-membrane lipid-asymmetry maintenance. In mycobacteria the paralogous YrbE proteins come in pairs (YrbE1A/1B to YrbE4A/4B) encoded in the four mce operons, and they are the permeases of importers for host-derived apolar lipids: deleting YrbE1A blocks fatty-acid uptake and deleting YrbE4A blocks cholesterol uptake. In plants and algae the orthologous permease TGD1 works with TGD2 and TGD3 at the chloroplast inner envelope to import ER-derived lipid, and it is a chloroplast envelope protein rather than a plasma-membrane one. PANTHER's family name is a generic ABC-permease descriptor and its SF4 name is taken from the plant member, so neither conveys that the family is overwhelmingly bacterial: the InterPro slice records 25930 proteins across 11877 proteomes in four subfamilies, while the fetched entries.csv covers only 14 reviewed members (enterobacterial/Haemophilus MlaE, a set of Rickettsia and cyanobacterial/red-algal orthologs, and Arabidopsis TGD1).
document.coherence_reason: All members are the membrane-embedded permease of an MCE-type lipid translocator, and that is enough to make the generic terms (plasma membrane for the bacterial members, lipid transport, ABC transporter complex) safe. Two groups diverge in ways that matter for propagation. The mycobacterial YrbE permeases, split by PANTHER across SF4 (the A subunits) and SF13 (the B subunits), serve importers whose substrates are fatty acids (Mce1) and cholesterol (Mce4), so phospholipid-specific terms do not hold for them even though they sit in the same subfamily as MlaE. The plant/algal TGD1 clade, also inside SF4, resides in the chloroplast envelope, which is why PAINT already carries an IRD removing the plasma-membrane term from the Viridiplantae branch. The divergence therefore cuts across subfamilies rather than along them, and is recorded here as member exceptions.

document.preferred_name: MCE-domain substrate-binding subunits: E. coli MlaD and the mycobacterial Mce/Lpr proteins of the mce1-mce4 lipid importers
document.summary: Substrate-binding subunits built around the MCE (mammalian cell entry) domain, which oligomerizes into a ring that projects from the inner membrane into the periplasm or cell-wall compartment and carries lipid through it. The reference member, Escherichia coli MlaD, is anchored in the inner membrane by a single N-terminal helix and forms an SDS-resistant homohexamer whose soluble domain binds endogenous phospholipids; within MlaFEDB it caps the MlaE permease (PTHR30188) and modulates the MlaF ATPase (PTHR43023), and cryo-EM shows the lipid pathway running from the MlaE site through the MlaD ring into the periplasm. MCE proteins are ubiquitous in double-membraned bacteria and in chloroplasts and absent from monoderms. Mycobacteria are the extreme case of expansion: each of the four mce operons encodes six MCE proteins (Mce1A-F and so on, several of them lipoproteins named LprK/LprL/LprM/LprN), which are thought to assemble heterohexameric rings with long needle-like projections spanning the thick mycobacterial envelope. Those systems are importers of host-derived apolar lipids - Mce1 for fatty acids, Mce4 for cholesterol - energized by a single shared ATPase, MceG, and they are virulence determinants: the family name "mammalian cell entry" comes from a 1993 experiment in which an M. tuberculosis DNA fragment conferred on E. coli the ability to invade HeLa cells. PANTHER splits the family into six subfamilies, five of them defined by mycobacterial Mce paralog position within the operon. The InterPro slice records 42662 proteins across 9713 proteomes, while the fetched entries.csv covers only six reviewed members.
document.coherence_reason: The shared property is architectural rather than functional: an MCE domain that oligomerizes into a lipid-conducting ring attached to an ABC transporter. Beyond that, the family lumps at least three functionally distinct groups. (i) MlaD and its diderm-bacterial orthologs bind phospholipids and work in outer-membrane lipid asymmetry maintenance. (ii) The mycobacterial Mce proteins of SF15-SF19, and the mycobacterial members of SF4, are substrate-binding subunits of importers for host fatty acids and cholesterol, located in the cell wall rather than at the plasma membrane, with roles in host interaction and persistence; phospholipid-specific terms do not hold for them. (iii) Within that mycobacterial set, only the Mce1 clade has any evidence bearing on host-cell entry, and the actinobacterial relatives in Streptomyces coelicolor - a soil saprophyte with no host - inherit host-interaction terms they cannot possibly perform. Subfamily boundaries follow operon position, not function, so SF4 contains both E. coli MlaD and mycobacterial Mce1D/Mce2D/Mce3D/Mce4D.

document.notes:
Written to support the Mla module's MlaD part (modules/bacterial_mla_intermembrane_phospholipid_transport.yaml), which selects PANTHER:PTHR33371:SF4 with the PSEPK exemplar Q88P92. All node ids, asserted terms, seeds, taxa and snapshot dates are verbatim from the cached PTHR33371-paint.tsv (one assessment per row, five rows); subfamily labels are verbatim from interpro/panther/panther.obo; member accessions come from PTHR33371-entries.csv or from UniProt cross-reference queries, with each representative member's subfamily read from its own UniProt DR PANTHER lines. Propagation counts quoted in the assessments were checked in QuickGO on 2026-10-23 (PTN002120837: 153 annotations across three terms; PTN002530749: 60 across two).
This is the most heterogeneous of the three Mla families, and the reason is structural: PANTHER's subfamilies are defined by position within the mycobacterial mce operon (A, B, C, D, E/lipoprotein, F), so each subfamily contains one position from all four operons - fatty-acid, cholesterol and two uncharacterized systems - while the canonical MlaD proteins share SF4 with the four Mce*D proteins. There is therefore no subfamily whose scope corresponds to "Mla phospholipid system", and that is why the phospholipid term assessments carry member exceptions inside their own applicable subfamily. A future PAINT curator wanting to fix this properly would place IRDs on the actinobacterial Mce clade for GO:0120010 and GO:0120014 and let GO:0006869 or GO:0005319 serve those members.
The GO:0044409 row is the clearest over-propagation found here: a host-invasion process reaching the MCE proteins of a non-pathogenic soil bacterium from a single M. tuberculosis seed whose own support is a 1993 heterologous invasion assay. It is assessed TOO_DEEP on the node, and the term assessment is left UNRESOLVED rather than scoped to a subfamily, because whether any member genuinely participates in host entry (as opposed to being required for persistence through lipid acquisition) is a question the cached literature does not settle.
No residue_sites: the boundaries here are substrate, compartment and lifestyle, all clade properties. The MCE ring's lipid conduit is formed by the hexamer's pore-lining loops rather than by a small set of identifiable residues, and no claim in this review or the member gene reviews turns on a position.

document.preferred_name: MlaB STAS-domain accessory subunit of the MlaFEDB transporter, plus uncharacterized MlaB-like STAS proteins
document.summary: Small (about 100-residue) cytoplasmic STAS-domain proteins (Pfam STAS_2, PF13466). The characterized subfamily, SF1, is MlaB: the cytoplasmic accessory subunit of the MlaFEDB ABC transporter of the Mla intermembrane phospholipid transport system. In E. coli MlaB (P64602) binds the nucleotide-binding domain MlaF, is needed for MlaF stability and for assembly of the MlaFEDB complex, and is required for transporter ATPase activity (the T52A substitution leaves the MlaFEB assembly intact but abolishes ATPase activity); its loss gives the same outer-leaflet phospholipid accumulation and SDS-EDTA sensitivity as other mla mutants. MlaB does not itself bind or move phospholipid; the lipid pathway runs through MlaE and the MlaD hexamer. SF1 is almost entirely gammaproteobacterial (Enterobacterales, Pasteurellales, Vibrio, Xanthomonas) with some Betaproteobacteria. SF2 ("BLR2341 PROTEIN", after Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens blr2341) is the larger and far more diverse subfamily: STAS proteins across Gamma-, Beta- and Alphaproteobacteria, Leptospira, Thermodesulfobacteriota, and also monoderm Actinomycetota and Bacillota, mostly named "STAS domain-containing protein" or "anti-sigma factor antagonist" by automatic pipelines; a few are named as Mla MlaB components, but none has been studied. InterPro counts 6988 proteins (integrated entry IPR052746); UniProt maps about 3400 of them to a subfamily. The fetched entries.csv holds the 3 reviewed members, all SF1.
document.coherence_reason: The family joins a characterized Mla accessory subunit (SF1) with a larger set of uncharacterized STAS proteins (SF2) that includes members in monoderm phyla (Actinomycetota, Bacillota) that have no outer membrane and therefore cannot take part in intermembrane phospholipid transfer. Whether any SF2 proteins act in Mla-like systems, in anti-sigma-factor-antagonist partner-switching, or in something else is unknown. Because STAS domains are a generic small-protein interaction fold, sequence membership alone does not carry the MlaB function across the family. All four PAINT terms sit on one gammaproteobacterial node inside SF1, so no term currently reaches SF2.

node_assessments.assessment_reason: The seed does not support an inherited function at this or any node. The only experimental basis is an acts_upstream_of_or_within IMP from a transposon screen in which a yrbB (mlaB) insertion made E. coli more readily killed by the quinolone nalidixic acid (PMID:20128927). Increased lethality of a DNA-gyrase poison in an envelope-defective mutant is an indirect, pleiotropic phenotype of outer-membrane lipid asymmetry loss, not evidence that MlaB participates in sensing or repairing DNA damage; the authors themselves group yrbB with outer-membrane-related genes. No other member has any DNA-damage data. Every SF1 member below the node currently inherits the term and should not.
